documentTexts:
Git Architecture: Three Trees & Snapshot Model
1. Working Directory: Untracked and tracked active files on local disk.
2. Staging Area (Index): Concrete snapshot cache prepared for the next commit.
3. Local Repository: Immutable Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) of cryptographically signed commits.
Mechanism: Commits store full tree snapshots addressed by 40-character SHA-1 hashes, not delta differences.
Core Git Snapshot Operations
1. git init: Initializes a new .git directory structure.
2. git add <path>: Moves modified files from working directory into the index/staging area.
3. git commit -m '<message>': Seals the staging area into a permanent commit node with parent pointers.
4. git status: Inspects differences between the working tree, staging area, and HEAD.
Branching, Merging & HEAD Pointer Mechanics
1. Git Branch: Lightweight movable reference pointer to a specific commit hash (41 bytes).
2. HEAD: Special symbolic reference pointer indicating the currently checked-out branch or commit.
3. Fast-Forward Merge: Moves the branch pointer forward linearly when no divergence exists.
4. 3-Way Merge: Creates a synthetic merge commit with two parents when divergent histories exist.
5. Merge Conflict: Occurs when identical lines are edited incompatibly across divergent branches.
Remote Collaboration & Distributed Sync
1. git remote add origin <url>: Establishes named alias pointing to central host (GitHub/GitLab).
2. git push -u origin <branch>: Pushes local commits and tracks upstream remote branch.
3. git fetch: Downloads remote commits and branches without altering local working files.
4. git pull: Automatically executes git fetch followed by git merge FETCH_HEAD.
Reset, Revert & Safe History Manipulation
1. git reset --soft HEAD~1: Moves HEAD pointer back; leaves index and working directory untouched.
2. git reset --mixed HEAD~1 (default): Moves HEAD and un-stages files; leaves working tree intact.
3. git reset --hard HEAD~1: Destructively resets HEAD, index, and working tree to previous state.
4. git revert <hash>: Creates a new forward-moving commit that inverts the targeted commit changes.
5. Detached HEAD: State where HEAD points directly to a commit hash rather than a named branch.

questions.questionText: Which statement accurately describes what the git commit command does?
options: It stores only the differences between the current and previous versions, not a full snapshot.
It moves modified files from the working directory into the staging area.
It uploads the local commits to the remote repository.
It creates a new snapshot of the staged files and records a commit message describing the changes.
questions.correctAnswer: It creates a new snapshot of the staged files and records a commit message describing the changes.
questions.explanation: According to the technical specification, git commit seals the staging area into a permanent commit node that stores a full tree snapshot identified by a SHA-1 hash, and the accompanying commit message documents the changes. Uploading to a remote is done by git push, staging files is done by git add, and commits store full snapshots, not just deltas.

questions.questionText: Which statement accurately contrasts a fast‑forward merge with a 3‑way merge and correctly identifies when a merge conflict occurs?
options: A fast‑forward merge is used only for remote branches, while a 3‑way merge is used only for local branches; merge conflicts arise when the repository exceeds 1 GB.

A fast‑forward merge moves the branch pointer forward when there is no divergence, whereas a 3‑way merge creates a new merge commit with two parents when histories have diverged; a merge conflict occurs when identical lines are edited incompatibly on the divergent branches.
Both fast‑forward and 3‑way merges always produce a merge commit, and merge conflicts only happen when binary files are changed.
A fast‑forward merge creates a new merge commit with two parents, while a 3‑way merge simply moves the branch pointer forward; a merge conflict occurs when the branches have no common ancestor.
questions.correctAnswer: A fast‑forward merge moves the branch pointer forward when there is no divergence, whereas a 3‑way merge creates a new merge commit with two parents when histories have diverged; a merge conflict occurs when identical lines are edited incompatibly on the divergent branches.
questions.explanation: According to the technical specification, a fast‑forward merge simply advances the branch pointer linearly when no divergence exists. When histories have diverged, Git performs a 3‑way merge, creating a synthetic merge commit with two parents. A merge conflict arises when the same lines are edited incompatibly across the divergent branches.
